name: build_bundle
title: Build a portable circuit
description: Author a feedforward circuit, write a bundle and check that it can be planned.
intro: Start here to learn the authoring boundary. Two input channels drive four conductance-based leaky integrate-and-fire cells through an AMPA projection. The script compiles this graph, writes a bundle, reloads it and asks the graph executor to plan it. It does not run the dynamics.
details:
## What to notice

1. Inputs declare symbolic time and batch axes; concrete dimensions arrive when you execute the graph.
2. The timestep and membrane time constant are explicit time quantities. Graph execution requires `COBA_LIF(tau_mem=...)`.
3. Projection weights are conductances in uS, and `NonNegative()` declares their constraint.
4. `compile()` validates and serializes authoring objects; `plan_graph()` checks the execution topology. Neither call is a simulation.

The output directory contains `feedforward.bundle/graph.json`, its manifest and a Markdown summary. Reloading verifies the bundle's declared digests, and the example asserts that the restored graph is unchanged. Graphviz is unnecessary because this example does not request diagram rendering.
output:
Bundle round-trip: identical graph
Plan: 1 population, 1 projection

name: poisson_circuit
title: Simulate a driven E/I circuit
description: Generate seeded Poisson input and inspect a small excitatory/inhibitory circuit.
intro: Drive an eight-cell excitatory population and a two-cell inhibitory population with four Poisson input channels. The PING component authors the recurrent E/I connections, and an explicit graph request runs 100 ms on CPU. The script reports retained spike tensor shapes and mean population firing rates, then saves the outputs in a NumPy archive.
details:
## What to notice

1. `executor="graph"` selects graph-native execution; the typed request otherwise defaults to the legacy route.
2. A timestep of 0.1 ms and 1,000 steps give a 100 ms presentation. A single supplied rate is broadcast across input channels.
3. Input generation and parameter initialization have explicit seeds. Changing either seed changes the experiment.
4. The reported rate is total spikes divided by presentation count, population size and duration in seconds. It is a population mean rather than the rate of a selected cell.

`activity.npz` contains `dt_ms`, `excitatory_spikes` and `inhibitory_spikes`. The spike arrays have time, batch and cell axes. This small illustrative run does not establish sustained oscillation or a scientific PING acceptance criterion. Exact observed rates can vary with library/backend changes.
output:
excitatory_spikes: shape=(1000, 1, 8), mean rate=30.0 Hz
inhibitory_spikes: shape=(1000, 1, 2), mean rate=90.0 Hz

name: replay_inputs
title: Replay dense and sparse spikes
description: Express one input stream in two representations and verify identical counts.
intro: Use four known spikes across two presentations and two channels to learn input binding without neuron dynamics. The same stream is represented first by a dense tensor and then by integer event coordinates. A time reduction returns raw counts per channel, and assertions compare both results to counts you can verify by hand.
details:
## What to notice

1. Dense spike tensors use time, batch and channel axes. Each value here is either zero or one.
2. Sparse coordinates are zero-based and ordered by step, batch and channel; duplicate coordinates are rejected.
3. `steps_count` and `batch_size` describe the whole presentation, including positions with no spikes.
4. A direct sum reduction produces raw channel counts. The `SpikeCount` readout additionally applies a learned linear projection, so it is a different operation.

With a 1 ms timestep and three steps, each presentation lasts 3 ms. Presentation zero contains two spikes on channel zero and one on channel one; presentation one contains one spike on channel one. Each invocation is a fresh run over the complete stream. Runtime continuation is a separate contract.
output:
Counts per presentation and channel: [[2.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0]]
Dense and sparse outputs match exactly

name: train_readout
title: Train a two-class readout
description: Fit a tiny synthetic fixture, save its checkpoint and run inference.
intro: Train a weighted spike-count readout to distinguish activity on input channel zero from activity on channel one. The four presentations are generated in memory, so no dataset download is needed. The script checks that cross-entropy decreases, saves the trained parameters and runs inference through the saved checkpoint.
details:
## What to notice

1. `TrainSpec` declares the objective, complete parameter scope, optimizer and physical presentation duration. Targets and sample tensors belong to the execution request.
2. The linear readout starts at zero. AdamW learns signed projection weights; this is an operation rather than an AMPA conductance projection.
3. `updates=10` means ten optimizer updates. This fixture uses the complete four-presentation batch.
4. Inference uses the checkpoint's parameters without resuming the optimizer. `argmax` converts the two scores into predicted class indices.

This intentionally simple task exercises the training interface. It has no hidden spiking population and therefore does not demonstrate surrogate-gradient learning through a spike threshold. Predictions are checked on the same fixture used for training; they are not a held-out accuracy measurement. For experiment design, add a separate evaluation protocol and dataset split.
output:
Cross-entropy decreases from approximately 0.6931.
Predictions: [0, 1, 0, 1]
Labels:      [0, 1, 0, 1]

name: resume_training
title: Save and resume training
description: Compare four uninterrupted updates with a two-plus-two checkpoint resume.
intro: Run the same small readout training job in two ways: four uninterrupted updates, and two updates followed by a checkpoint reload and two more updates. The script compares final parameters, optimizer state and the resumed loss records exactly on CPU.
details:
## What to notice

1. A checkpoint records completed optimizer updates as well as named parameters, optimizer state and authenticated execution metadata.
2. When resuming, `updates=2` requests two additional updates. The resumed update numbers are three and four.
3. The graph, training recipe, inputs, target binding and seed remain consistent across the two routes. Authentication rejects incompatible continuation requests.
4. Training checkpoints and dynamic simulation runtime states solve different problems. A runtime state retains voltages, conductances, histories and refractory counters; this example resumes optimizer training.

The assertions establish equality for this deterministic CPU fixture on the current implementation. They do not establish equality between CPU and accelerator trajectories or between different numerical environments. The script is independent of the preceding training example and builds its own graph and fixture.
output:
Resumed from update: 2
Final parameters, optimizer state and resumed losses match exactly

name: plot_recording
title: Plot retained activity
description: Create a spike raster and membrane-voltage figure from actual simulation outputs.
intro: Simulate six COBA-LIF cells driven by alternating spikes on two input channels. Convert the actual output tensors into a validated Recording, then use FigureGrid to place a spike raster above a mean-voltage trace. The example saves both the figure and its retained numerical evidence.
details:
## What to notice

1. Output tensors include a batch axis. This example has one presentation and explicitly selects it before constructing the Recording.
2. `Recording.require()` fails if a requested signal is absent. The plotting code consumes the stored arrays rather than rerunning the simulation or filling missing signals.
3. Raster positions use source steps multiplied by the 0.1 ms timestep. The trace averages voltage across the six cells, not across repeated trials.
4. FigureGrid uses named regions with normalized figure coordinates. Matplotlib's Agg backend exports a PNG without an interactive display.

The output directory contains `recording.png` and `recording.npz`, with `dt_ms`, `spikes` and `voltage` in the archive. Input channels spike every 10 ms, offset by 5 ms. The preview below was generated by this script with seed 17; it is one illustrative simulation, not an aggregate or uncertainty estimate.
output:
Recording: 1000 steps, 100.0 ms
Exported recording.png and recording.npz
